extracted.intended_audience: mathematical-competition organizers, teachers, university enrichment coordinators, and local/national Tournament of the Towns committees
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and standards for running, expanding and participating in the Tournament of the Towns: rules for rounds and scoring, problem-style expectations, translation/coordination procedures, organisational roles (local/national/central), resources, and enrichment activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition schedule (twice-yearly rounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tournament was organised to take place twice yearly — November (northern Autumn) and March (northern Spring) — with distinct Autumn and Spring rounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rounds are scheduled to allow repeated participation; simultaneity and hemisphere differences must be considered when expanding internationally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Town scoring adjusted by population
rubrics_metrics.description: A town's score is based on N papers where its population is N×100,000. A minimum of 5 papers is required and towns with population less than 500,000 receive a further compensating adjustment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This adjustment enables small towns to compete on an equal basis with large cities and reduces provincial isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problems should be non-standard and test pure problem-solving
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems are typically non-standard, often challenging, and are intended to test sheer problem solving ability rather than technical syllabus knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem style favors clever, memorable constructions ("masterpieces") that can become part of competition folklore; examples include combinatorial and tiling puzzles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem authorship and sourcing via Kvant (curated selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many of the best problems come from past winners and contributors connected with Kvant; new problems are traditionally sent to Kvant where a competent team selects the best for the Tournament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using an established editorial/selection process helps maintain high problem quality and continuity of style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation quality: international language committees
rubrics_metrics.description: Translation of problems into other languages has caused difficulties due to long or non-standard formulations; the recommendation is to set up an international committee for each major scientific language (including native speakers) to approve the version in that language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An approvals committee ensures identical wording (e.g., American and Australian versions), reducing ambiguity and unfairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simultaneity and scheduling across hemispheres
rubrics_metrics.description: Finding convenient dates for all participating countries is difficult because of differing academic years in southern hemisphere countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If papers are guaranteed to be available, southern-hemisphere participants could schedule close dates; organizers should coordinate dates to minimize conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central coordination / uniform assessment (jurisdiction of Moscow jury)
rubrics_metrics.description: Central assessment (historically by Moscow) is needed to supervise uniform standards across participating towns; currently papers are marked by Moscow State University students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As the Tournament grows, establish further juries or distribute assessment responsibilities while maintaining central coordination to ensure uniformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local preliminary checking and forwarding best papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Local committees should perform preliminary local checking of papers and forward the best pupils' papers to the central committee (Moscow) for coordination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This two-stage marking (local pre-check + central coordination) preserves local engagement while ensuring consistent final standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish national committees and their responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: National committees (example: Bulgaria, Australia) are charged to attract new participating towns, submit problems, edit booklets with problems, and make awards to top participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: National committees may also handle translation, final checking, coordinating of papers, and inclusion in national competition calendars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordination of checking criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a need to coordinate the criteria used when checking participants' papers to ensure comparable marking across towns/countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: National committees should align local marking rubrics with central standards and communicate checking conventions to local markers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjustable difficulty and beginner accommodations
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns about level of difficulty lead to proposals such as allowing participants to choose 3 questions out of 5 or 6 or having a separate special round for beginners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offering choice or beginner rounds can broaden accessibility while preserving high-level challenges for experienced contestants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enrichment centres structure and role
rubrics_metrics.description: Universities and mathematicians can run enrichment centres with open sessions (Term 1–3) and invitational groups (all terms), splitting students into junior and senior groups during competition terms and practicing past papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invitation membership should be reviewed annually; centres provide lectures, practice, and act as preparation hubs for Tournament participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summer conferences and winners' gatherings
rubrics_metrics.description: Winners gather at summer conferences (e.g., Estonia, Beloretsk) where advanced problems are solved and the conference of leaders meets to discuss problems; outcomes can be published for broader distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conferences serve both pedagogical and organisational purposes and help disseminate problem ideas and organisational best practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universities as organising foundations and staffing needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Universities staff typically organise regional Tournament activity; to realise a greater programme, positions (akin to tenured faculty) are needed to perform pedagogical, scientific and administrative work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stable institutional positions and involvement helps sustain long-term development and coordination of activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material resource requirements (hardware and administration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organisers need PCs (AT or higher), printers (LQ or laser), photocopying equipment, facsimile machines, e-mail and office space to process questions, solutions and results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of hardware is a major bottleneck; western assistance or modest entry fees could help fund required equipment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensation and support for student markers and volunteers
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics students at universities contribute significantly to marking and organisation and should be compensated for their work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compensation and formal support improves sustainability of marking and reduces reliance on unpaid volunteer labour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and dissemination of past papers and solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish translated past problems with strategy essays and solutions; larger, more complete collections are desirable for preparation and historical record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Books and booklets assist training, preserve problem folklore, and standardise problem exposure across countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain problem-creation role of original organisers while expanding
rubrics_metrics.description: When widening the organisational base internationally, care should be taken not to diminish the role of those currently successful in problem creation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expansion should complement, not replace, the creative team responsible for producing high-quality problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social and extracurricular programme as part of the Tournament
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tournament's greater programme can include tourist trips, musical activities, construction/volunteer groups, ecological schools, and other social activities alongside mathematical events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such activities build camaraderie and show mathematicians' ability to cooperate in varied settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nominal entry fee to support operations in Western entries
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically no entry fee was charged, but in western countries students expect to pay (~$2) and a modest fee could raise funds to support organisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charging a small fee in western countries could provide sustainable funds for resources and administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem formulation length and clarity (translation-sensitive style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems may have long, non-standard formulations which create translation difficulties and potential confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem authors and translators should aim for clarity; approved translations and editorial oversight can mitigate misinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need to establish additional juries as participation grows
rubrics_metrics.description: Growth of the Tournament demands extra juries beyond Moscow to handle increased workload while retaining some central oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New juries can ease marking load; central coordination is still needed to guarantee uniform standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internationally approved exams for different participant roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposal to set up an internationally approved set of exams for 'maths pupil', 'maths student' and 'maths teacher'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standardised exams would help benchmark participants and teachers across countries and support the greater programme's pedagogical aims.
